doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

chapter: Growing up and discovering Latin music
title: Learning the real Latin feel from Frankie Malabe and Louie Ramirez
summary: Getting the bass-on-the-one puzzle, Frankie Malabe teaching conga rhythms on his knees, and learning arranging from Louie Ramirez's band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: You mentioned the Miles Davis that you put away for a year and then you got it out again and you literally had a “bing.” Did you have to have a bing with absorbing the Latin rhythms and sort of getting it inside you?

In a way yes. ‘Cause that first gig that I mentioned to you where it was just a quartet playing Tito Puente arrangements, I couldn’t understand at the very beginning in Latin music the bass player does not play on the one, and that’s all the music I ever heard, the bass always played on the one. But on Latin music they play on the one and — one two three four one two boom bing, boom boom. That kind of rhythm. And I remember playing the first couple of songs and I was really thrown off, I was reading the music but trying to figure out how come what I was playing was in 4/4 but that didn’t sound like what the bass was playing. As soon as that hooked up, that was a milestone for me. Because then I started to appreciate that that was also what the conga player was playing on, and that’s what the clave was all about. So slowly but surely I started finding out those things as a result. I was very lucky, you know, Monk, that my introduction to the real deal of Latin music was brought about by two wonderful musicians. One was a conga player named Frankie Malabé, and one was a timbale player/arranger named Louie Ramirez. And Frankie would have me come to his house. He knew that I liked Latin music. I knew that he liked jazz. So he would come to my house and we would put on my collection and listen to that. When I went to his house, he lived on Simpson Street, which was, you know the famous Fort Apache Precinct, well that was on Simpson Street. It was across the street, about six, seven houses down. And I would go to his house, his father- in-law was a great cook by the way, he used to have rice and beans, he always had it for me. The main thing is I appreciated good food. And what Frankie would do is he would set up two chairs facing each other and we would be knee to knee. And he would play music, Latin music, and play on my knees what he would play as a conga player, and explain why. With Louie Ramirez, Louie was a great arranger. So just by playing in his band and absorbing how he approached the rhythms and what he wrote for the horns, and

that was my introduction to that end of the music. And like I said, I was always asking questions to make sure I knew exactly that I was getting the real deal, and I was lucky enough to have had those two fellas as my teachers.
Yeah you couldn’t pay for that kind of thing in a music school I don’t think.
